subject: physics
question_text: Derive an expression for the centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The setup
lines: A body moves on a circle of radius r with
constant speed v. In a time Δt the radius
turns through an angle Δθ, and the velocity
vector turns through the SAME angle Δθ.
steps.why: The velocity always stays perpendicular to the radius, so when one turns by an angle the other must turn by the same angle.
common_mistakes: Assuming the velocity vector does not turn because the speed is constant.

recall.must_convey: That in time delta t the radius and the velocity both turn through the same angle delta theta.
accept: both turn through the same angle
radius and velocity turn by delta theta

steps.label: The similar triangles
lines: The triangle of the two velocity vectors and
the triangle of the two radii are similar,
both being isosceles with the same apex
steps.why: Similar triangles turn a hard vector subtraction into a ratio of lengths, which is the whole method of this derivation. Here Δs is the chord between the two positions; for a very small Δt the chord equals the arc, so Δs/Δt becomes the speed v.
common_mistakes: Writing Δv / r = Δs / v, the two triangles matched up wrongly.

recall.must_convey: That the velocity triangle and the radius triangle are similar, giving delta v by v equals delta s by r.
accept: delta v by v equals delta s by r
reject: both turn through the same angle

steps.label: The result

lines.text: a = v²/r = ω²r,  towards the centre

lines: The speed never changes; only the direction
does, so this acceleration is always
steps.why: An acceleration perpendicular to the velocity can only turn the motion, never speed it up — which is why the speed stays constant.
common_mistakes: Dropping the direction; the magnitude alone does not earn the last mark.

recall.must_convey: That a equals v squared by r, equal to omega squared r, directed towards the centre.
